## Introduction

This example fits a background cosmology to baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from
SDSS DR16 using NumCosmo. We will:

1. define a cosmological model,
2. choose which parameters are free,
3. create a distance calculator for BAO observables,
4. load several BAO likelihoods,
5. build a dataset and likelihood,
6. run the fit and inspect the covariance,
7. optionally continue with an ensemble MCMC analysis.

## Prerequisites

Before running this example, make sure the `numcosmo_py`[^numcosmo_py] package is installed in your
environment. If it is not already installed, follow the
[installation instructions in the NumCosmo documentation](https://numcosmo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html).

This example uses the core NumCosmo Python bindings, together with `numpy`, `pandas` and
`plotnine` for the figures. The optional MCMC visualization uses `getdist`, as in the
[SN Ia fitting example](snia.qmd).

## Import and Initialize

First, import the required modules and initialize the NumCosmo library. The `Nc` and
`Ncm` modules provide the core NumCosmo functionality. The call to `Ncm.cfg_init()`
initializes the library objects.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

# These modules must be loaded before getdist to avoid its side effects
import numcosmo_py.plotting
import getdist
from getdist import plots

from numcosmo_py import Nc, Ncm
from numcosmo_py.plotting import mcat_to_catalog_data

Ncm.cfg_init()
```

## Set Up the Cosmological Model

We use the homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model `NcHICosmoDEXcdm`. As in the
[H(z) example](hz.qmd), we rewrite the dark energy density parameter in terms of the
curvature parameter.

```{python}
# Initialize the cosmological model
cosmo = Nc.HICosmoDEXcdm()

# Rewrite Omega_x in terms of Omega_k
cosmo.omega_x2omega_k()
```

## Set Parameter Values

We now assign initial values to the cosmological parameters. These values provide the
starting point for the fit.

```{python}
cosmo["H0"] = 70.0
cosmo["Omegab"] = 0.05
cosmo["Omegac"] = 0.25
cosmo["Omegak"] = 0.0
cosmo["w"] = -1.0
```

## Choose the Free Parameters

BAO measurements are ratios: they constrain $D_M/r_d$ and $D_H/r_d$, never absolute
distances. The sound horizon at the drag epoch, $r_d$, is set by the physical densities
$\Omega_b h^2$ and $\Omega_m h^2$, so fixing $H_0$ and $\Omega_b$ pins it and the measured
ratios act as absolute distances. We keep $H_0$ fixed here and fit $\Omega_c$ and $w$; the
[H(z) example](hz.qmd) leaves $H_0$ free instead, because cosmic chronometers measure
$H(z)$ directly rather than through $r_d$.

We free $w$ alongside $\Omega_c$. With a single free parameter the covariance matrix is a
scalar and the ensemble sampler below would have nothing two-dimensional to explore.

```{python}
cosmo.props.H0_fit = False
cosmo.props.Omegac_fit = True
cosmo.props.w_fit = True
```

## Create the Distance Calculator

BAO likelihoods depend on cosmological distance quantities. We create a `Distance`
object prepared for calculations up to redshift $z = 3$, which covers the Lyman-$\alpha$
samples near $z \approx 2.3$.

```{python}
# Create a distance object optimized up to redshift 3
dist = Nc.Distance(zf=3.0)
```

## Build the Model Set

We now create a model set from the cosmological model. The model set is the container
used by NumCosmo to connect model parameters with likelihood calculations. Once the free
parameters have been chosen, `prepare_fparam_map` builds the map from the model's
parameters to the vector the fit actually varies.

```{python}
# Create a model set containing the cosmological model
mset = Ncm.MSet.new_array([cosmo])

# Build the free-parameter map and show the resulting configuration
mset.prepare_fparam_map()
mset.pretty_log()
```

`pretty_log` prints a second model below the cosmology, `NcBBN`, which the model set
carries by default to supply the primordial helium abundance. It has no free parameters
here and is not fitted; its presence does not mean the model set was built wrongly.

## Select the BAO Samples

NumCosmo provides many predefined BAO likelihoods through `Nc.DataBaoId`. The following
cell lists every identifier available in the current installation, together with the
number of data points and a short description.

```{python}
# List the available BAO dataset identifiers with basic metadata
for _, member in sorted(Nc.DataBaoId.__enum_values__.items()):
    name = member.value_name.replace("NC_DATA_BAO_", "")
    data = Nc.data_bao_create(dist, member)

    print(f"{name:40s}  n = {data.get_length():2d}  {data.get_desc()}")
```

This example uses the six SDSS DR16-era likelihoods. To use a different combination,
replace the identifiers below by any of those printed above.

```{python}
# BAO likelihoods used in this example
bao_samples = [
    Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR12_2016_DR16_COMPATIBLE,
    Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR16_LRG_2021,
    Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR16_QSO_2021,
    Nc.DataBaoId.EMPIRICAL_FIT_1D_SDSS_DR16_ELG_2021,
    Nc.DataBaoId.EMPIRICAL_FIT_2D_SDSS_DR16_LYAUTO_2021,
    Nc.DataBaoId.EMPIRICAL_FIT_2D_SDSS_DR16_LYXQSO_2021,
]
```

## Build the Dataset and Likelihood

We now create the dataset from the selected BAO likelihoods and use it to construct the
likelihood.

```{python}
# Create a dataset holding all selected BAO likelihoods
dset = Ncm.Dataset.new_array(
    [Nc.data_bao_create(dist, bao_id) for bao_id in bao_samples]
)

# Create the likelihood from the dataset
lh = Ncm.Likelihood(dataset=dset)
```

## Create and Run the Fit

We now create a `Fit` object. In this example, we use the NLOpt backend with the
`ln-neldermead` algorithm. The fit combines the likelihood, the model set, and a
numerical differentiation method.

We run it with `run_restart` rather than `run`. Nelder-Mead is a simplex method: the
simplex contracts around a point and can stall before reaching the true minimum.
`run_restart` re-minimizes from the previous optimum with a fresh simplex and repeats
until an entire minimization improves $-2\ln L$ by less than a tolerance. Its arguments
are the message level, the absolute tolerance (`1.0e-3`), the relative tolerance (`0.0`,
i.e. unused), and two optional arguments for saving the model set to a file, left as
`None` here.

```{python}
# Create the fit object
fit = Ncm.Fit.factory(
    Ncm.FitType.NLOPT,
    "ln-neldermead",
    lh,
    mset,
    Ncm.FitGradType.NUMDIFF_FORWARD,
)

# Run the fit, restarting until the minimum stops improving
fit.run_restart(Ncm.FitRunMsgs.SIMPLE, 1.0e-3, 0.0, None, None)
fit.log_info()
```

The `m2lnL` printed above is $-2\ln L$, and on this dataset it is not a $\chi^2$ offset by
a constant. Three of the six likelihoods are tabulated $-2\ln p$ curves carrying their own
normalizations, as the next section describes, so there is no Gaussian normalization to
subtract and no $\chi^2$ per degree of freedom to read off the printed value. It is useful
for comparing fits to this same dataset, not as a goodness-of-fit statistic.

## Estimate the Covariance Matrix

After finding the best-fit point, we estimate the covariance matrix for the free
parameters.

The choice of method is forced by the data. Three of the six likelihoods above are
tabulated $-2\ln p$ curves --- `EMPIRICAL_FIT_1D_SDSS_DR16_ELG_2021` and the two
`EMPIRICAL_FIT_2D_*` Lyman-$\alpha$ samples --- which carry no Gaussian mean vector. The
*expected* Fisher matrix, `Ncm.Fit.fisher`, is built by differentiating that mean vector,
so it cannot be used when any member of the dataset lacks one. `Ncm.Fit.obs_fisher`
instead differentiates $-2\ln L$ itself and works for every likelihood here. The
[SNIa + BAO example](rg_snia_bao.qmd) discusses the difference between the expected and
observed information in detail.

```{python}
# Observed information: numerical Hessian of -2lnL, valid for empirical likelihoods
fit.obs_fisher()

# Print the covariance matrix
fit.log_covar()
```

The `relative tolerance not reached` message above is expected here rather than a sign of
failure. Three of the six likelihoods are tabulated $-2\ln p$ curves, so the numerical
Hessian is differentiating an interpolated function whose second derivatives are poorly
determined; the worst relative error stalls near $2.5 \times 10^{-1}$ instead of reaching
the $10^{-5}$ target. The MCMC below estimates the same covariance by sampling instead of
differentiation and reproduces it closely, which is what confirms the result.

The small uncertainty on $w$, and its distance from $-1$, are conditional on the assumed
$H_0$ and $\Omega_b$ through $r_d$, and should not be read as a measurement of the
equation of state.

## Compare the Best-Fit Model with the Data

After the fit, the cosmological model holds the best-fit parameters, so we can plot the
quantities the likelihood evaluates against the measurements themselves. Three of the six
samples --- the DR12 consensus and the DR16 LRG and QSO samples --- report $D_M/r_d$ and
$D_H/r_d$ at a given redshift, eight numbers in total. The other three are tabulated
$-2\ln p$ curves and have no mean value to plot.

Each of those three datasets stores the pair $(D_M/r_d,\, D_H/r_d)$ per redshift,
interleaved in one vector with the redshift repeated across the pair. The curves come from
`Dt_r` and `DH_r`, the same `Distance` methods the BAO likelihood calls, so the model and
the data are the same dimensionless ratios by construction and no unit conversion enters.

```{python}
# | label: fig-bao-model-vs-data
# | fig-cap: Best-fit model (line) against the eight distance-ratio measurements. Error bars are marginal $1\sigma$; the $D_M$--$D_H$ correlation within each sample is not shown.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

# Prepare the distance calculator with the best-fit cosmology
dist.prepare(cosmo)

# The three samples that report distance ratios directly
ratio_samples = [
    ("SDSS DR12", Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR12_2016_DR16_COMPATIBLE),
    ("SDSS DR16 LRG", Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR16_LRG_2021),
    ("SDSS DR16 QSO", Nc.DataBaoId.DTR_DHR_SDSS_DR16_QSO_2021),
]

# Even entries are D_M/r_d, odd entries D_H/r_d; errors are the square root of the
# covariance diagonal
data_rows = []
for sample_name, bao_id in ratio_samples:
    data = Nc.data_bao_create(dist, bao_id)
    cov = data.peek_cov()
    z_i = data.props.z.dup_array()
    mean_i = data.peek_mean().dup_array()

    for i, (z, mean) in enumerate(zip(z_i, mean_i)):
        sigma = np.sqrt(cov.get(i, i))
        data_rows.append(
            {
                "z": z,
                "value": mean,
                "ymin": mean - sigma,
                "ymax": mean + sigma,
                "quantity": "D_M/r_d" if i % 2 == 0 else "D_H/r_d",
                "sample": sample_name,
            }
        )

bao_data_pd = pd.DataFrame(data_rows)

# Model curves on a redshift grid covering the measurements
z_a = np.linspace(0.05, 2.5, 200)
bao_model_pd = pd.concat(
    [
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "z": z_a,
                "value": [dist.Dt_r(cosmo, z) for z in z_a],
                "quantity": "D_M/r_d",
            }
        ),
        pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "z": z_a,
                "value": [dist.DH_r(cosmo, z) for z in z_a],
                "quantity": "D_H/r_d",
            }
        ),
    ]
)

(
    ggplot(bao_model_pd, aes("z", "value"))
    + geom_line()
    + geom_errorbar(
        data=bao_data_pd,
        mapping=aes(x="z", ymin="ymin", ymax="ymax", color="sample"),
        inherit_aes=False,
        width=0.05,
    )
    + geom_point(
        data=bao_data_pd,
        mapping=aes("z", "value", color="sample"),
        inherit_aes=False,
        size=2,
    )
    + facet_wrap("quantity", scales="free_y")
    + labs(x=r"$z$", y="", color="Sample")
    + doc_theme()
)
```

The model tracks the measurements across the whole range. The largest single departure is
the DR16 LRG $D_H/r_d$ point, about $2\sigma$ below the curve.

::: {.callout-note}
## Optional advanced section

The next sections extend the BAO best-fit analysis with an ensemble MCMC sampler. They
are not required for the basic BAO fit above, but they show how the same likelihood and
model set can be reused for posterior sampling.
:::

## Configure the Initial Sampler

The fit above gives the best-fit point and an approximate covariance matrix. We can also
continue the analysis with an ensemble Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler, which samples the
parameter space around the best fit and provides another estimate of the uncertainties.

The ensemble sampler needs an initial distribution for the walkers. Here we use a Gaussian
transition kernel seeded with the covariance computed above, so the initial ensemble
already has roughly the right shape.

```{python}
# Create a Gaussian transition kernel for the initial sample
init_sampler = Ncm.MSetTransKernGauss.new(0)

# Associate the sampler with the model set
init_sampler.set_mset(mset)

# Use the model-set parameter information to define the prior
init_sampler.set_prior_from_mset()

# Start the walkers from the best-fit covariance
init_sampler.set_cov(fit.get_covar())
```

## Configure the Ensemble Walker

The ensemble sampler evolves several walkers in parallel through parameter space. In
this example, we use the APES walker, which builds proposal distributions from the
current ensemble.

```{python}
# Number of walkers in the ensemble
nwalkers = 300

# Create the APES walker
walker = Ncm.FitESMCMCWalkerAPES.new(nwalkers, mset.fparams_len())
```

## Create the Ensemble Sampler

We now combine the fit object, the initial sampler and the ensemble walker into an
`Ncm.FitESMCMC` object, which controls the MCMC run.

Two settings are worth noting. `set_use_threads` lets the sampler evaluate the ensemble in
parallel; the number of threads comes from OpenMP, so it follows `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and the
machine's core count rather than any NumCosmo setting. And `set_rng` fixes the random seed:
without it the sampler draws its own seed at `start_run`, and every render of this page
would produce different numbers and a different posterior plot. Parallel evaluation does
not compromise this --- the random draws are made serially, and only the likelihood
evaluations are threaded.

```{python}
# Create the ensemble MCMC object
esmcmc = Ncm.FitESMCMC.new(
    fit,
    nwalkers,
    init_sampler,
    walker,
    Ncm.FitRunMsgs.NONE,
)

# Evaluate the ensemble in parallel
esmcmc.set_use_threads(True)

# Fix the seed so this page is reproducible across renders
esmcmc.set_rng(Ncm.RNG.seeded_new("mt19937", 1234))
```

## Run the Ensemble MCMC

We can now run the ensemble sampler. It initializes the chain, advances a fixed number of
ensemble steps, and closes the run. Each step advances all `nwalkers` walkers, so 200 steps
produce 60000 sampled points. A fixed step count keeps the cost of building this page
predictable, but it is not a convergence criterion: the first steps are still relaxing away
from the initial ensemble and are discarded as burn-in below.

```{python}
# Start the MCMC run
esmcmc.start_run()

# Run a fixed number of ensemble steps
esmcmc.run(200)

# Finish the MCMC run
esmcmc.end_run()
```

## Inspect the MCMC Results

Before using the chain we discard the burn-in: `trim` drops every point earlier than the
given ensemble step, here the first 20 of 200. Its second argument is a thinning factor,
and `1` keeps every remaining row. The mean and covariance are then computed from the
trimmed catalog and stored in the fit object, so they print in the same format used above.

```{python}
# Access the MCMC catalog and discard the first 20 ensemble steps
mcat = esmcmc.peek_catalog()
mcat.trim(20, 1)

# Compute the MCMC mean and covariance from the trimmed chain
esmcmc.mean_covar()

# Print the covariance estimated from the MCMC sample
fit.log_covar()
```

These numbers agree closely with the ones above: the parameter values to within a fifth
of a standard deviation, the uncertainties to within about 3%. That agreement indicates
the posterior is close to Gaussian over this range. The two estimates are not the same
quantity --- `obs_fisher` gives a quadratic approximation at the maximum, while
`mean_covar` reports the posterior mean and width --- and they separate once the posterior
is broad or asymmetric, as in the [H(z) example](hz.qmd).

## Visualize the MCMC Posterior

Finally, we can visualize the MCMC samples. The triangle plot shows the marginalized
posterior distributions for the two fitted parameters and their joint confidence regions.
GetDist reports `Removed no burn in` because the burn-in was already removed from the
catalog in the previous step.

```{python}
# | label: fig-bao-mcmc-results
# | fig-cap: MCMC posterior samples for the BAO SDSS DR16 fit.
# | fig-cap-location: margin
# | code-fold: true

# Convert the trimmed NumCosmo catalog to a GetDist-compatible object
cd = mcat_to_catalog_data(mcat, name="BAO SDSS DR16 fit")

# Plot the marginalized and joint posterior distributions
g = plots.get_subplot_plotter()
g.triangle_plot(cd.to_mcsamples(), shaded=False, filled=True)
```

## Summary

In this example, we fitted BAO measurements from SDSS DR16 with an XCDM background
cosmology. The basic workflow followed the standard NumCosmo fitting structure:

1. create a cosmological model,
2. set initial parameter values,
3. choose the free parameters,
4. create a distance calculator,
5. select the BAO likelihoods,
6. build the dataset and likelihood,
7. run the fit,
8. estimate the covariance matrix.

We then extended the same setup with an optional ensemble MCMC analysis. This second
part reused the likelihood and model set from the best-fit calculation, configured an
initial sampler and an ensemble walker, and used the resulting chain to estimate the
posterior mean and covariance.

In this example, $\Omega_c$ and $w$ were varied in the fit, while $H_0$ and the other
cosmological parameters were kept fixed. The same structure can be extended to include
additional BAO samples, other cosmological models, or more free parameters.
